summary: Specifies a mechanism for Proxy Mobile IPv6 that creates a transient binding cache entry to improve handover performance for dual radio and single radio handovers. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: When a phone hops between networks, there is a gap in connection. This creates a temporary entry so traffic reaches it faster during the move.

questions: what is transient binding in pmipv6
how does transient binding reduce packet loss
subtitle: Optimizing handovers in Proxy Mobile IPv6 with temporary dual forwarding.

tldr.problem: When a mobile device hands over to a new network in Proxy Mobile IPv6, the local mobility anchor immediately switches all traffic to the new access gateway. If the device's new interface is not ready to receive packets yet, packets are delayed or lost.
tldr.mechanism: A transient binding cache entry maintains forwarding paths to both the old and new access gateways during handover. Downlink traffic continues to the old gateway until the new interface is ready, while uplink traffic is accepted from both gateways.
tldr.outcome: Handover becomes smoother with reduced packet loss and delay, supporting both single-radio and dual-radio mobile devices.

today: RFC 6058 is an Experimental protocol that extends Proxy Mobile IPv6. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and remains a reference for network implementers seeking to optimize PMIPv6 handovers.

sections.title: The Handover Problem
sections.content:
Proxy Mobile IPv6 (PMIPv6) is a network-based mobility protocol that lets mobile devices move between networks without handling mobility signaling themselves. When a mobile node (MN) hands over from one Mobility Access Gateway (MAG) to another, the Local Mobility Anchor (LMA), which acts as a central router, must update the mobile node's Binding Cache Entry (BCE) to point to the new MAG.

The problem occurs because the mobile node's new interface may not be immediately ready to receive data. According to the base PMIPv6 specification, the LMA switches forwarding to the new MAG as soon as it receives the Proxy Binding Update (PBU) message. But in reality, the device must first attach to the new network, request and receive an IP address via router discovery, perform address configuration, and possibly set up security. This process can take more than one second. During this delay, packets sent by the LMA to the new MAG are either buffered (consuming resources) or lost entirely.

Similarly, uplink packets from the old MAG may still arrive at the LMA after the binding has been updated, causing them to be dropped because the LMA now only accepts traffic from the new MAG.
sections.eli5: PMIPv6 networks automatically let your device move between base stations. But when you switch base stations, your device needs time to set itself up on the new one. The network immediately forgets about the old base station, so data meant for you gets lost or stuck.

sections.title: Transient Binding Cache Entries
sections.content:
RFC 6058 introduces the concept of a transient binding cache entry as a solution. Instead of immediately updating the binding to point only to the new MAG, the LMA maintains a temporary state that keeps two forwarding entries in the BCE: one for the old MAG (pMAG) and one for the new MAG (nMAG).

During the transient state, the LMA behaves differently for uplink and downlink traffic:

  • Uplink: The LMA accepts packets from both the old and new MAGs. If uplink packets from the old link arrive late (due to slow links), they are still accepted and forwarded.
  • Downlink: The LMA continues forwarding packets to the old MAG until the new interface is ready. This is called a late path switch. It is particularly useful for dual-radio handovers where the old interface remains active, or for single-radio handovers where radio-level forwarding mechanisms can be reused.

The transient BCE has a lifetime, after which it is converted to a normal (active) BCE. This conversion can be triggered by a timeout, an explicit signal from the new MAG, or a deregistration message from the old MAG.
sections.eli5: Instead of instantly switching, the network keeps both paths alive for a short time. Data going down to you keeps going through your old base station until your new one is ready. Data going up from you is accepted on both paths so none gets lost.

sections.title: How Transient Binding Works
sections.content:
The handover sequence with transient binding involves two phases: initiation and activation.

Phase 1: Initiation — When the mobile node attaches to the new MAG, the new MAG sends a PBU with a Transient Binding option to the LMA. This signals that a transient binding should be created. Alternatively, the LMA can decide on its own to enter transient state and signal this decision in the Proxy Binding Acknowledgment (PBA) to the new MAG. The LMA now maintains both forwarding paths and enters the transient state. The new MAG marks the MN's binding as transient in its binding update list, knowing that the binding will eventually need to transition to active.

Phase 2: Activation — The transient BCE is converted to an active BCE when the new interface is ready. This can happen in several ways: the new MAG can send a PBU without the Transient Binding option (signaling that IP configuration is complete), the LMA can activate based on a timeout, or the old MAG can send a deregistration. Once activated, the LMA switches the downlink forwarding path to the new MAG exclusively.

Between these two phases, the precise behavior depends on how the transient binding is configured. The Transient Binding option specifies whether a late path switch (L) should be used, allowing continued downlink forwarding to the old MAG during the transient period.
sections.eli5: Step 1: The new base station tells the network to create a temporary two-path setup. Step 2: When the phone is ready on the new base station, the network stops using the old path and switches to the new one.

sections.title: The Transient Binding Option
sections.content:
RFC 6058 defines a new Transient Binding mobility option that is carried in PMIPv6's PBU and PBA messages. This option allows both the new MAG and the LMA to signal and configure transient binding behavior.

The option includes the following information:

  • Status field: Indicates whether the option is requesting initiation of a transient BCE, confirming transient state, or requesting activation (transition to active).
  • Late path switch (L) flag: Specifies whether downlink traffic should continue to be forwarded via the old MAG during the transient state.
  • Maximum lifetime: Specifies how long the transient state may persist. The new MAG may propose a lifetime based on its knowledge of address configuration delays, and the LMA may override this with its own value.

The option is placed in the PBU by the nMAG to propose transient binding, or in the PBA by the LMA to accept or modify the transient binding parameters. The presence or absence of the option in subsequent PBU messages from the nMAG signals whether activation should occur.
sections.eli5: A new message field tells the network: 'Use both paths for now', 'Keep sending down the old path', and 'How long should this last'.

sections.title: Implementation Considerations
sections.content:
Implementation of transient binding requires changes at both the LMA and the MAGs. The LMA must be able to maintain multiple forwarding entries per binding and apply different forwarding rules (unidirectional or bidirectional) to each entry. It must also manage the transient state lifetime and transition to active state when appropriate.

The new MAG must be able to detect when a transient binding is appropriate (e.g., via link-layer indications that a handover is underway), decide whether to propose transient binding in the PBU, estimate a reasonable lifetime, and signal activation when the mobile node's new interface is ready to receive data.

The old MAG remains largely transparent to the transient binding operation; it continues to forward packets normally until explicitly deregistered.

RFC 6058 notes that even without transient binding, some static configuration (such as allowing the LMA to temporarily accept uplink traffic from both old and new MAGs) could help. However, the dynamic transient binding solution is more flexible and adapts better to different handover scenarios and access technologies.
sections.eli5: The network devices need to be smarter about keeping track of both paths and when to switch. The phone does not need to know anything special; the network handles it all.
